records.text: The Hall family owned land and were clothiers. They ran the whole business of making cloth, from sheep farmers and shearers to weavers, fullers and buyers. Around 1610 John Hall and his wife Elizabeth built The Hall on medieval foundations, facing a river that powered the family's fulling mills and, later, its looms.
records.source_title: Who Were The Halls?
records.source_author: The Hall / Alex Moulton Charitable Trust
records.uncertainty: The page gives no author or date; the year comes from the URL path. Historic England's listing names the builder as John Hall II, c.1610. The page says the family's landholding may go back to 1170, and marks this only as possible.

records.text: Historic England's garden listing says that when John Hall II died in 1631 the house went to Rachel Baynton. She married into the Pierrepoint family, later Dukes of Kingston, and the house was renamed Kingston House. By the late 1700s the owners seldom lived there and it served as a farmhouse.
records.source_title: The Hall, Bradford-on-Avon (Register of Parks and Gardens, list entry 1001233)
records.source_author: Historic England
records.uncertainty: Written in 2000 and edited up to 2004. Conflicts with the Moulton Trust page, which says the last Hall to live there died in 1710 and left the house to his illegitimate daughter Rachel Baynton.

records.text: In 1805 Thomas Divett, a City of London man, bought the estate. He replaced an old corn mill southwest of the house with a cloth mill and used the house itself as a wool store. The mill later failed in a slump in the town's cloth trade, and the house and land were put up for sale in 1848.
records.source_title: The Hall, Bradford-on-Avon (Register of Parks and Gardens, list entry 1001233)
records.source_author: Historic England
records.uncertainty: VCH Wiltshire vol. 7 dates Divett's purchase to 1802. VCH vol. 4 says the five-storey Kingston mill was built in 1811 and stood idle from 1842.

records.text: Bradford's clothmaking shrank fast after about 1815. There were about 19 manufacturers in 1820, 14 in 1826 and only 5 by 1833. The town kept to broadcloth while export demand for it fell, and by 1838 it had just four mills employing 418 people.
records.source_title: Textile industries since 1550, VCH Wiltshire vol. 4
records.source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
records.uncertainty: The Moulton Trust gives 32 factories in 1800 and 5 in 1838; the sources may be counting different things.

records.text: In the early 1840s fashion moved towards bright, lightweight, intricately woven fabrics, and demand for the town's traditional cloth fell. Then in 1841 the local bank failed. It had invested heavily in two of the largest mills. More than 400 workers were hit, the workhouse could not cope, and many people left to find work.
records.source_title: What Happened To The Woollen Trade?
records.source_author: The Hall / Alex Moulton Charitable Trust
records.uncertainty: VCH vol. 4 names the bank as Hobhouse & Co., which failed in autumn 1841.

records.text: In 1791 about 500 cloth workers gathered at Westbury House, the home of clothier Joseph Phelps, to protest against a new scribbling machine. Shots fired at the crowd killed three people, one of them a child. The crowd then burned the machine on the town bridge. The coroner ruled the killings justifiable and awarded Phelps £250.
records.source_title: Poverty and protest (review of Rosie MacGregor, Remnants and Yarns)
records.source_author: Andrew Eberlin, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
records.uncertainty: Casualty figures differ between sources (three dead including a child; or one killed and two mortally wounded).
records.check_note: Source says shots were fired at the crowd, not that they came from the house. Fixed.

records.text: There were disputes over pay before the machine riots. The town's first recorded riot, in November 1726, was against more work for less pay. In 1787 weavers rioted over wages. The clothiers reportedly promised not to build bigger loom shops if the weavers accepted lower rates.
records.source_title: Poverty and protest (review of Rosie MacGregor, Remnants and Yarns)
records.source_author: Andrew Eberlin, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
records.uncertainty: The 1787 promise is reported second-hand.

records.text: In 1803 women made up about two-fifths of the weavers in Bradford and Trowbridge. Across the county that year, a working day of 13 to 16 or even 17 hours was not unusual, and weavers put their own pay at roughly 7s 6d to 10s a week.
records.source_title: Textile industries since 1550, VCH Wiltshire vol. 4
records.source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
records.uncertainty: Hours and wages are county-wide figures, not Bradford alone.
records.check_note: Source says 13 to 16 or even 17 hours; wages are the weavers' own estimates. Fixed.

records.text: Numbers 1 to 18 Middle Rank are a terrace of weavers' houses built in the late 1600s. Most are two storeys with attic rooms in the gables and stone-mullioned casement windows. Part of the row has since been rebuilt. The terrace was listed Grade II in 1963 for its value to the townscape.
records.source_title: 1-18 Middle Rank (listed building entry)
records.source_author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
records.uncertainty: Entry amended 1974; the rebuilding is described only as 'recent'.

records.text: Stephen Moulton was Charles Goodyear's agent. He brought the first samples of vulcanised rubber to Britain and shared them with Thomas Hancock, who won the British vulcanisation patent in 1843, a few weeks ahead of Goodyear. Disputes over patents and rights followed, and in 1848 Moulton started his own firm at Kingston Mill.
records.source_title: S. Moulton and Co
records.source_author: Grace's Guide to British Industrial History
records.uncertainty: The page does not say how Hancock used the samples. VCH vol. 4 adds that Moulton had his own 1847 patent.

records.text: Moulton's start-up depended on American partners and skills. He made an 1847 agreement with the Rider brothers and James Thomas of New York. In 1848 an American engineer, Mr Frost, oversaw the machinery, and an American foreman and forewoman, S. P. Abbot and Amelia Fisher, followed him. Woollen workers who had lost their jobs supplied the local labour.
records.source_title: Other industries, VCH Wiltshire vol. 4
records.source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
records.uncertainty: The VCH says the Riders were partners for four years from 1850.

records.text: Bradford on Avon Museum says Moulton was backed by Goodyear and by his friend Septimus Palairet of Woolley. He picked the town for its empty powered mills and its workers already used to factory work. He supplied buffers, springs and hoses to Brunel's Great Western Railway, and rubber-coated cloth for army capes after the Crimean War began in 1853.
records.source_title: Rubber Industry
records.source_author: Bradford on Avon Museum
records.uncertainty: Undated page. The Moulton Trust names the backer 'Captain Palairet of Woolley Grange'.

records.text: The Moulton works specialised in rubber for engineering, above all railway springs, bearings, and buffer and draw-bar springs. It also made hose, tubing, belting, washers and valves. Output of springs and rings alone rose from about £3,600 in 1857 to nearly £58,000 by 1890.
records.source_title: Other industries, VCH Wiltshire vol. 4
records.source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
records.check_note: Source table is of output, not sales. Fixed.

records.text: The Moulton firm's workforce started small and grew slowly: 78 people in 1850, only 52 in 1875, 164 by 1900 and 793 by 1950.
records.source_title: Other industries, VCH Wiltshire vol. 4
records.source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
records.uncertainty: Moulton Trust claims almost everyone in town worked there over 150 years; against these figures that is a generalisation.

records.text: The 'Iron Duke' calender, named after Wellington, was designed in America and built in Britain in 1849 for Kingston Mill. It pressed rubber onto woven cloth to make waterproof sheeting. When Avon demolished the mill in 1972, the machine went to Bristol's new Industrial Museum. It was put back on show at the site in 2016.
records.source_title: UK puts 19th century rubber calender on display
records.source_author: European Rubber Journal
records.uncertainty: Grace's Guide dates the machine c.1848 and its removal to 1973.

records.text: George Spencer was testing rubber for railway springs and shock absorbers. He judged Moulton's product the best for the purpose and set up his own firm in the early 1850s. In 1891 the two businesses merged as George Spencer, Moulton and Co.
records.source_title: George Spencer, Moulton and Co
records.source_author: Grace's Guide to British Industrial History
records.uncertainty: VCH vol. 4 dates Spencer's London firm to 1853.

records.text: New Mills, now part of the Kingston Mills group, was built as a woollen mill by James Harper and Thomas Taylor, with 1869 carved on its pediment. Cloth-making there stopped in 1898. Soon afterwards Spencer, Moulton and Co took over the empty buildings and converted them for rubber around 1900. Rubber was made there until 1992.
records.source_title: New Mills (Buildings 72-75), Kingston Mills (listed building entry)
records.source_author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
records.uncertainty: The neighbouring listing says Spencer Moulton bought New Mills in 1899; the 2012 town trail says rubber continued until 1994.

records.text: Abbey Mill on Church Street was built as a cloth mill by Richard Gane for Harper, Taylor and Co, and stopped making cloth in 1898. It was later used mainly by the rubber firms Spencer Moulton and then Avon. After the factory closed in 1995, the building was converted into retirement apartments.
records.source_title: Bradford on Avon Town Trail
records.source_author: Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust, Museum and TIC
records.uncertainty: Build date given as 1874 or 1875; end of cloth 1898 or 1902. VCH vol. 4 says Spencer Moulton bought the mill in 1926.

records.text: Greenland Mills housed the Sirdar Rubber Works. Sirdar went bankrupt in 1914, and in 1915 the Avon India Rubber Company took over the works and about 300 workers. Avon had started in a run-down cloth mill at Limpley Stoke and later moved to Melksham.
records.source_title: Avon India-Rubber Co
records.source_author: Grace's Guide to British Industrial History
records.uncertainty: Greenland Upper Mill may have made woollen cloth until 1906, so cloth and rubber may have shared the Greenland buildings.

records.text: In January 1956 the Avon India Rubber Company of Melksham bought Spencer Moulton outright. The Bradford firm kept its name, and a plan was made to move Avon's general rubber goods production to the Bradford works.
records.source_title: Other industries, VCH Wiltshire vol. 4
records.source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
records.uncertainty: The History Centre says Alex Moulton left the firm in 1956.
records.check_note: Source records the plan but not its date or whether it was carried out. Fixed.

records.text: The Spencer Moulton archive at the Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre covers the firm from its founding in 1848 to the Avon takeover in 1956. Cataloguing had by then covered more than 240 volumes, including a nearly complete run of wage books from 1850 to the 1940s, and some 3,600 plans, and photographs of products such as railway buffers.
records.source_title: Breaking the Mould: Cataloguing the archives of Spencer Moulton and Dr Alex Moulton
records.source_author: Tom Plant, Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre
records.uncertainty: No catalogue reference numbers given.

records.text: Margaret Dobson's book A Vanished World recalls the Kingston Mill rubber works at the centre of town. Anyone crossing the Town Bridge passed it, and its hooters could be heard all over town. When it closed in 1992, staff were offered jobs at other company sites, but local shops and pubs lost much of their trade.
records.source_title: A Vanished World by Margaret Dobson (book review)
records.source_author: Angela and David Moss, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
records.uncertainty: Closure dates vary across sources from 1991 to 1995; different buildings probably closed at different times.

records.text: Former workers remembered constant dirt from soot and carbon black, and a separate canteen room for men covered in black powder. Some jobs, such as checking the bounce of every tennis ball, were very dull. Smoking in the workshops could get you sacked, so breaks were taken outside by the river. A Works Committee existed from 1918.
records.source_title: A Vanished World by Margaret Dobson (book review)
records.source_author: Angela and David Moss, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
records.uncertainty: Most of the memories are undated.

records.text: Linden Homes Western redeveloped the former rubber factory site as Kingston Mills. The scheme, designed by Nash Partnership, has 171 converted and new homes plus shops, a café and restaurant space. In 2012 it won Best Mixed Use at the Sunday Times British Homes Awards.
records.source_title: Linden Homes wins Sunday Times award for historic riverside development
records.source_author: Linden Homes
records.uncertainty: Developer's own release. An ecology report records bat colonies on site; the Moulton Trust says the factory was demolished in 2011.

records.text: The name Bradford comes from a wide ford over the Avon, which flows westward through the parish. The crossing served routes running north and south, and the ford stayed in use alongside the later stone bridge until the nineteenth century.
records.source_title: Bradford on Avon (Community History)
records.source_author: Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre, Wiltshire Council
records.uncertainty: Writing date inferred.

records.text: Town Bridge began in the 1200s as a packhorse crossing, possibly replacing an earlier bridge. Two of its original pointed, ribbed arches survive at the south end on the east side, and in 1400 the Pope supported an appeal for alms to pay for repairs.
records.source_title: The Town Bridge (List Entry 1036011)
records.source_author: Historic England
records.uncertainty: An earlier bridge may have stood here; Wiltshire Council says the first stone bridge was Norman.

records.text: A small square domed building on the bridge, probably of the 1600s, was used as the town lock-up in the eighteenth century and known as a blind house. A stone vault inside forms two cells, and its gilded copper fish weathervane, the Bradford Gudgeon, may be sixteenth-century.
records.source_title: The Town Bridge (List Entry 1036011)
records.source_author: Historic England
records.uncertainty: Dates given only as probable. Other sources say the lock-up replaced a medieval bridge chapel.

records.text: The bridge was only about ten feet wide until its width was doubled in 1768-9. The lock-up on its upstream side began as a medieval bridge chapel, which the antiquary John Aubrey noted on a visit, and was later rebuilt, perhaps to hold prisoners briefly.
records.source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
records.source_author: Royal Archaeological Institute; Pam and Ivor Slocombe
records.uncertainty: Historic England places the widening in the 17th century.

records.text: Barton Bridge is a fourteenth-century former packhorse bridge with four pointed arches reaching a small island, and three triangular cutwaters on its upstream face. A narrower footbridge over a side stream was added in the mid-1800s, and a Second World War pillbox stands on the island.
records.source_title: Barton Bridge (List Entry 1364494)
records.source_author: Historic England
records.uncertainty: The cutwaters may be later medieval additions; many facing stones date from a late-19th-century repair.

records.text: The great barn was probably built in the 1330s for Barton Grange, a manor farm of Shaftesbury Abbey, a very wealthy Dorset nunnery. The abbey acquired Bradford's rectory and its tithes in 1332, hence the tithe-barn label; a smaller barn about 43 metres long preceded it around 1300.
records.source_title: History of Bradford-on-Avon Tithe Barn
records.source_author: English Heritage
records.uncertainty: No document confirms the build date; what the barn stored is unclear.
records.check_note: Source says manor farm, not home farm. Fixed.

records.text: Shaftesbury Abbey held a large estate centred on Bradford from about 1001 through the Middle Ages, managed from Barton. Tree-ring dating places the great barn's two-tier cruck roof between 1334 and 1379, the barn was standing by 1367, and the nearby granary dates to 1370-90.
records.source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
records.source_author: Royal Archaeological Institute; Pam and Ivor Slocombe
records.uncertainty: Tree-ring dating gives a range; the grant date is approximate.

records.text: William of Malmesbury reported the church standing in the 1120s and linked it to St Aldhelm, who died in 709. Its architecture instead points to building in the early eleventh century for the Shaftesbury nuns after the 1001 grant; its rich carving may relate to relics of Edward the Martyr.
records.source_title: Saxon Church of St Laurence
records.source_author: National Churches Trust
records.uncertainty: Dating disputed: Aldhelm c.700, early 11th century, or late 10th century. The relics link is speculative.
records.check_note: Source says Malmesbury reported the church standing; it doesn't say he saw it. Fixed.

records.text: Canon Jones of Holy Trinity identified the forgotten building in 1856 after reading William of Malmesbury. Other buildings had boxed it in, the chancel had been turned into a three-storey cottage, its arch replaced by a chimney built from the same stones, and an upper room held a school.
records.source_title: Church of St. Laurence, Bradford on Avon
records.source_author: Wiltshire Council Community History
records.uncertainty: Another account credits carved angels found in 1856 repairs; one town website gives 1871.

records.text: The council-backed visitor website says the Saxon Church of St Laurence dates from about AD 700 and was found only in 1871. It also says Saxons had reached the area by 652 and that the town grew around the river ford.
records.source_title: History of Bradford on Avon
records.source_author: Explore Bradford on Avon (Bradford on Avon Town Council)
records.uncertainty: Popular summary; conflicts with sources favouring a late 10th/early 11th-century building rediscovered in 1856.

records.text: During 2016 renovation and flood-protection work at Holy Trinity, on the Avon's north bank, archaeologists found early burials under the boiler-house floor, one cut by the 12th-century nave. Radiocarbon dated two to roughly the 800s-900s, pointing to an earlier church, perhaps Aldhelm's minster of about 705.
records.source_title: New evidence for a lost church
records.source_author: Wessex Archaeology
records.uncertainty: The link to Aldhelm's minster is a hypothesis; radiocarbon ranges are broad.

records.text: In 652 Cenwalh, king of Wessex, fought a battle at a place recorded as Bradonforde be afne, the earliest written reference to the town. By 705 a small monastery headed by St Aldhelm stood on the north-west bank of the river.
records.source_title: Bradford on Avon (Community History)
records.source_author: Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre, Wiltshire Council
records.uncertainty: The battle site is unlocated (possibly Budbury); the monastery's position is inferred, not excavated.

records.text: Budbury holds an Iron Age hillfort, partly excavated by Geoffrey Wainwright in the late 1960s, that may have been reused after Roman rule. A twelfth-century text names a battle at Wirtgeornsburh, meaning Vortigern's fort, possibly the West Saxon-British fight of 652.
records.source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
records.source_author: Royal Archaeological Institute
records.uncertainty: The identification with Budbury and with the 652 battle is tentative.

records.text: Teachers noticed lines of parched grass on St Laurence School's football pitch, matching buried walls. Excavations led by Mark Corney of Bristol University revealed two fourth-century Roman villas linked by a long corridor paved with a large mosaic of a vase between dolphins, probably made in Cirencester.
records.source_title: Mosaic news brief (Archaeology vol. 55 no. 6)
records.source_author: Jarrett A. Lobell, Archaeology magazine
records.uncertainty: A 2003 report dates the oldest parts to AD 230-270.

records.text: After Roman rule ended, a round baptistery about 15 feet across was cut into the reception-room mosaic of the eastern villa in the fifth century. The excavators called it the earliest known private chapel in post-Roman Britain; the villas were occupied from the 230s into the fifth century.
records.source_title: Unearthed: a luxury Roman villa with chapel (Daily Telegraph, via romanhideout.com)
records.source_author: David Derbyshire
records.uncertainty: The baptistery is an interpretation of a circular feature; the text is a copy on a secondary site.

records.text: Kingston Mill was built beside the Avon in 1807. In 1848 Stephen Moulton, who had bought the neighbouring Hall, turned the then-idle mill into a rubber factory. A textile mill close to the Hall drew its water through a leat channelled off the river.
records.source_title: Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire: archaeology and history (summer meeting notes)
records.source_author: Royal Archaeological Institute; Pam and Ivor Slocombe
records.uncertainty: The build date conflicts with other records (1805, 1811). The summary does not name the mill fed by the leat or say when it was dug.

records.text: Moulton chose the disused Kingston woollen mills for rubber-making in 1848 because empty factories already fitted for water and steam power stood ready, along with workers used to mill life. Early products included buffers, springs and hoses for the Great Western Railway.
records.source_title: Engineering & Industry
records.source_author: Explore Bradford on Avon (Bradford on Avon Town Council)
records.uncertainty: Unattributed tourism text; gives 1995 for the end of rubber production.

records.text: The weir near Avoncliff aqueduct, downstream of the town, holds back about two metres of water, and a local book suggests it dates from the late 900s. In 2020 engineers judged a breach likely, which could lower levels up to Greenland Mills by one to two metres, prompting community-funded emergency repairs.
records.source_title: Avoncliff weir repairs supported by community
records.source_author: Bradford on Avon Town Council
records.uncertainty: The 10th-century origin rests on one local book.

records.text: By the early 1500s Avoncliff had a mill on each bank of the Avon, grinding corn and fulling cloth. Around 1791 Moggeridge and Joyce installed water-driven cloth machinery there, perhaps the first locally; from the mid-1800s to the late 1930s both mills shredded old textiles into upholstery flock.
records.source_title: Westwood / Avoncliff (Community History)
records.source_author: Wiltshire Council Community History
records.uncertainty: The c.1791 installation was possibly, not certainly, the earliest in the area.

records.text: Avoncliff Aqueduct, designed by John Rennie, carries the Kennet and Avon Canal over the river on three tall segmental arches, the middle one highest. The canal was closed and drained in 1954 and reopened after restoration in the 1980s; the aqueduct was listed Grade II* in 1988.
records.source_title: Kennet and Avon Canal, Avoncliff Aqueduct (List Entry 1021876)
records.source_author: Historic England
records.uncertainty: Wiltshire Council gives construction as 1795-98; the Canal Trust gives 1990 for full reopening.

records.text: The aqueduct's central arch sags slightly, possibly because supporting centring was removed before mortar set or because porous limestone was damaged by frost during building. After the Great Western Railway bought the canal in 1852, cracked stonework was patched with blue brick; the Canal & River Trust later repaired it in harder matching stone.
records.source_title: John Rennie's Dundas and Avoncliff aqueducts
records.source_author: Victoria Owens, Rochester Bridge Trust
records.uncertainty: Two possible causes of the sag; no exact construction date.

records.text: The town has flooded repeatedly, including in 1925, 1932, 1960, 1968, 1979, 2000, 2003, 2013, 2014, 2023 and 2024; November 2024 brought the highest Avon level since local gauging began in 1998. The floodplain narrows from about 600 to 70 metres where the river cuts into town.
records.source_title: Briefing Note: Bradford-on-Avon community flood briefing
records.source_author: Environment Agency with Wiltshire Council, Wessex Water and Town Council
records.uncertainty: The listed years are examples, not a complete record (an 1882 flood level is marked in town).
